name: Chylous Ascites

criteria.description: Presence of milky, turbid ascitic fluid on paracentesis
Ascitic fluid triglyceride concentration >110 mg/dL (1.24 mmol/L)
Imaging evidence of lymphatic obstruction or leakage (e.g., lymphangiography, lymphoscintigraphy)
Exclusion of other causes of ascites such as malignancy, infection, or cirrhosis

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Milky ascitic fluid with elevated triglycerides (>110 mg/dL) plus exclusion of other causes of ascites
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is confirmed by biochemical analysis of ascitic fluid and supported by imaging studies.

laboratory: Elevated triglyceride concentration in ascitic fluid (>110 mg/dL)
imaging: Lymphangiography showing lymphatic obstruction or leakage
Ultrasound or CT scan demonstrating ascites with characteristic fluid density
genetic: No specific genetic markers identified; may be associated with congenital lymphatic malformations
other: Biochemical analysis excluding infection or malignancy

distinguishingFeatures: Ascitic fluid with malignant cells on cytology
Typically serous or hemorrhagic fluid rather than milky
Ascitic fluid with high protein and lymphocytes but not milky
Positive acid-fast bacilli or PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Systemic symptoms like night sweats and weight loss
Ascitic fluid is typically clear or straw-colored
History of liver disease and portal hypertension

references: Runyon BA. Management of adult patients with ascites due to cirrhosis: an update. Hepatology. 2009.
Browse NL, et al. Chylous ascites: a collective review. Surgery. 1982.
